distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer clinicopathologic disease leaf for urticarial lesions caused by small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Complement status, anti-C1q status, SLE association, hereditary complement deficiency, organ-threatening disease, and treatment response are represented as mechanisms, axes, risk/context factors, or future second-layer subtype context, not as disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking can use persistent urticarial wheals lasting more than 24 hours, pain or burning rather than pure itch, residual hyperpigmentation or purpura, angioedema, arthralgia, fever, complement consumption, anti-C1q positivity, skin biopsy leukocytoclastic vasculitis when the workup is available, and renal, pulmonary, ocular, or gastrointestinal involvement. Histology, complement studies, antibody testing, and treatment response remain structured evidence rather than hard labels.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Circulating immune complexes, often with anti-C1q antibodies in hypocomplementemic disease, activate the classical complement pathway and consume C1q, C3, C4, and CH50.
Immune-complex deposition and complement activation injure superficial dermal venules, producing urticarial plaques with biopsy evidence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
Histamine-mediated edema contributes to wheals and pruritus, but the vasculitic component makes lesions fixed, painful or burning, and incompletely antihistamine-responsive.
Neutrophils, eosinophils, nuclear dust, erythrocyte extravasation, and fibrinoid necrosis drive pain, purpura, hemorrhagic change, and residual pigmentation.

Autoreactive B-cell activity supports relapsing disease, anti-C1q antibody persistence, association with connective-tissue disease, and response to B-cell-directed treatment in refractory systemic cases.
When vasculitis extends beyond skin, fever, arthralgia, renal, pulmonary, ocular, gastrointestinal, cardiac, and neurologic complications become possible.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Renal immune-complex nephritis and vascular injury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Glomerular immune deposits or renal small-vessel vasculitis cause hematuria, proteinuria, active urinary sediment, creatinine rise, and long-term kidney risk.
Systemic urticarial vasculitis can involve lung parenchyma or airways, producing dyspnea, infiltrates, obstructive disease, alveolar hemorrhage, or respiratory failure.
Episcleritis, scleritis, uveitis, or conjunctivitis can accompany systemic disease and can threaten vision when severe or recurrent.
Bowel-wall small-vessel vasculitis can cause abdominal pain, bleeding, ischemic lesions, necrotizing vasculitis, and rare colectomy-level complications.

supportive_care: Document lesion duration, fixed location, pain or burning, itch, purpura, bruising, residual hyperpigmentation, angioedema, mucosal swelling, and photographs during active lesions.

Biopsy a fresh active lesion when diagnosis is uncertain; structure leukocytoclastic vasculitis, nuclear dust, neutrophilic infiltrate, erythrocyte extravasation, and fibrinoid necrosis as post-workup evidence.

Screen for systemic involvement with urinalysis, urine protein quantification, creatinine/eGFR, blood pressure, complement C3/C4/CH50/C1q, anti-C1q when available, inflammatory markers, and targeted autoimmune/infectious testing.
Track renal, pulmonary, ocular, and GI symptoms longitudinally; abdominal pain, dyspnea, hematuria/proteinuria, scleritis, or visual symptoms should raise organ-specific hazards.
Use antihistamines as symptom control only; persistent lesions over 24 hours, purpura, biopsy vasculitis, or systemic organ involvement should remain active disease evidence.
For dapsone, assess hemolysis/methemoglobinemia risk and G6PD status when relevant; monitor blood counts and oxygenation symptoms.
For hydroxychloroquine, document dosing, renal function, ocular baseline risk, and ophthalmology monitoring context.

For steroids and immunosuppressants, separate vasculitis activity from infection, screen for latent or active infection where relevant, and monitor glucose, blood pressure, bone risk, cytopenias, liver tests, and renal function.
Coordinate dermatology, rheumatology, nephrology, pulmonology, ophthalmology, gastroenterology, and surgery according to organ axes rather than subtype labels.
quality_notes: No first-line, preference, guideline, or indication-strength labels are encoded; treatment order must emerge from forward simulation and case context.
Hypocomplementemic, normocomplementemic, anti-C1q-positive, SLE-associated, and complement-deficiency contexts are represented as axes or modifiers under the pure disease leaf.
Systemic event hazards are included so renal, pulmonary, ocular, GI, infection, and mortality consequences can emerge through hazard drift rather than case-specific rules.
Antihistamine limitation is represented causally: histamine symptoms may improve while immune-complex vasculitis mechanisms and systemic hazards remain largely unchanged.
